title: Graphene Device Achieves Lossless Fractional Charge Conduction in Quantum Breakthrough
excerpt: University of Washington researchers demonstrate the first dissipationless fractional Chern insulator, conducting electricity along fractionally charged edges without losing energy to heat.
body:
• Researchers at the University of Washington have built the first device where electricity flows along fractionally charged edges with essentially zero energy loss — a long-sought state of matter called a dissipationless fractional Chern insulator.
  • The breakthrough, published in Nature Physics, eliminates the need for powerful magnetic fields by using twisted layers of molybdenum ditelluride to produce fractional charge behavior at zero field.
  • The advance opens a practical path toward fault-tolerant quantum computers that could process information with far greater resilience to errors.

A team of researchers at the University of Washington has demonstrated for the first time a device in which electrical current flows along fractionally charged edges without losing energy to heat — a milestone that brings one of quantum physics' most exotic phenomena closer to practical application.

The work, published in Nature Physics and led by physicist Xiaodong Xu, represents the first realization of a "dissipationless fractional Chern insulator," a state of matter that physicists have pursued for more than a decade. If the technology can be scaled, it could form the foundation for quantum computers that are inherently resistant to the errors that plague current designs.

Electrons That Split Into Fractions

In everyday materials, electrons behave as indivisible units of charge. But under extreme conditions — typically involving powerful magnetic fields and temperatures near absolute zero — electrons in two-dimensional materials can behave collectively, giving rise to quasiparticles that carry only a fraction of an electron's charge. This phenomenon, known as the fractional quantum Hall effect, was first observed in the 1980s and earned its discoverers a Nobel Prize in 1998.

https://x.com/EPFL_en/status/2089355326382330019

The challenge has been that the effect traditionally requires carefully maintained magnetic fields, making it impractical for real-world devices. A newer class of materials called fractional Chern insulators can exhibit the same fractional charge behavior at zero magnetic field — but until now, the effect always came with significant energy dissipation.

Engineering a Cleaner Device

Xu's team tackled the dissipation problem on two fronts. First, they developed a new crystal growth technique — horizontal flux growth — that boosted charge-carrier mobility by more than an order of magnitude compared to earlier experiments. Second, they refined the device fabrication process to reduce twist-angle disorder in the layered material.

"The initial discovery of the FQAH effect was exciting, but far from perfect. Although the Hall resistance was quantized at the expected value, the longitudinal resistance, which is expected to vanish, was still appreciable."

— Xiaodong Xu, University of Washington

The devices use two layers of molybdenum ditelluride, twisted relative to one another at a precisely chosen angle. When tuned to a state corresponding to two-thirds filling of the electronic band, the unwanted resistance nearly vanished — meaning electrical energy flowed along the material's edges with essentially no loss.

A Surprising Finding

The cleaner devices also revealed unexpected physics. The thermal activation gap — the energy barrier that protects the fractional state from disruption — was found to decrease as magnetic field strength increased, the opposite of what happens in traditional fractional quantum Hall systems. The researchers attribute this to a competition between different types of low-energy excitations tied to electron spin and charge.

Implications for Quantum Computing

The fractional charge states observed in these materials are of particular interest for topological quantum computing, an approach that would encode information in the collective behavior of quasiparticles rather than in individual quantum bits. Because the information is distributed across the system, it would be inherently more resistant to the decoherence that causes errors in conventional quantum computers.

The graphene-based platform demonstrated by MIT researchers in 2024 — using five stacked layers of graphene to achieve the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect — has added further momentum to the field, showing that multiple material systems can support these exotic states.

"The quantum Hall community has made repeated breakthroughs by improving sample quality over the last 40 years. Building on this experience, we hope that progress on this new platform will be even faster."

— Xiaodong Xu, University of Washington
